answers.answer: The client sends its request to the service entry point; the reverse-proxy balancer selects and forwards to a backend, which performs the application work and returns its response through the balancer to the client. Choose L7 for /search versus /purchase pools. It needs readable HTTP contents; HTTPS normally requires TLS termination at the proxy, while backend encryption is a separate choice. L4 typically selects for a TCP connection using network information rather than paths. Many HTTP requests can reuse that one connection and all reach the same backend without new selections. One adequate server may suffice when neither traffic distribution nor redundant serving is needed.

evidence.quote: The balancer forwards the request to a selected backend, which performs the operation and returns a response through the balancer to the client.
Path routing requires readable HTTP contents.
Many HTTP requests can reuse that connection. They can all reach the same backend; adding requests on that connection does not force new selections.
One adequate server may be enough if the service does not need traffic distribution or redundant serving.

answers.answer: Round robin takes turns among eligible backends; it is simple for similar servers and work, but a cheap lookup and long request each count as one, so equal turns need not mean equal work. Least connections prefers fewer active connections and can help with uneven durations, but one connection can carry much more work than another. Weights control traffic share: twice measured capacity could start at twice the weight, but configuration is neither a live capacity measurement nor a guarantee. Measure latency and resource use to choose. Adding an API backend cannot remove a saturated shared database bottleneck. After a machine failure, clients need a reachable alternate entry path through an available managed entry or redundant frontends with working, tested failover. Surviving backends need enough spare capacity for redirected load; otherwise visibly limit or reject excess work. Redundant boxes alone do not ensure availability.

evidence.quote: a quick read and a slow report still each count as one request.
Prefers the backend with fewer active connections.
A server with twice the measured capacity might start with twice the weight. Configured weights are not a live measurement or a performance guarantee.
More API servers can help when API processing is the bottleneck; they do not remove a saturated shared database bottleneck.
After one backend fails, the survivors need enough capacity for the remaining load.
If it fails, clients need a reachable alternate entry path, not just another disconnected balancer box.

answers.answer: A 200 from the health endpoint establishes that the endpoint answered, not that purchases can do useful work. Readiness checks should reflect the database capability required by the handler. Even improved checks have limited coverage, intervals, and failure thresholds, and failure may occur just after a successful probe, so detection takes time. Removal from eligible backends stops new selections, but it cannot complete, undo, or safely replay requests already underway, which can still fail. Also inspect the product all-unhealthy policy: some send to unhealthy targets if all fail checks.

evidence.quote: Readiness means it can accept useful new work: a process can answer /health while an application handler cannot reach its required database.
Checks have limited coverage, intervals and failure thresholds; a backend can fail just after passing. Detection takes time.
Once detected and removed from eligible backends, it stops receiving new selections. Requests already underway can still fail; removal does not complete, undo or safely replay them.

answers.answer: If the cart exists only in A memory, B cannot read it when a request lands there. If A fails, the only copy can be lost. Sticky routing prefers A for that customer and helps ordinary requests reach the cart, but can skew load and restrict placement. It does not copy the cart or guarantee survival of A failure. Shared session storage lets either backend read the cart, but adds access or coordination work and another shared dependency whose availability matters.

evidence.quote: If a server keeps a user's session only in A's memory, B cannot read it. Losing A can lose the only copy.
It can keep ordinary requests on A, but skew load and restrict placement. It does not copy the session or preserve it when A fails.
Lets either backend read the session. It adds access or coordination work and a shared dependency whose availability matters too.

answers.answer: Stop new assignments to A, manage existing connections or stop their further requests, and track accepted work. Allow the accepted 20-second request time to finish within a bounded deadline; then shut A down after completion or deadline expiry. New assignments are future work, whereas the accepted request is already underway and must be allowed and tracked during the drain. At the deadline, forced termination may interrupt unfinished work; it is not automatically moved to B. Stopping new L4 connections alone does not prevent further HTTP requests on the reused connection. Draining must handle connection lifetimes or further request acceptance for that routing unit; L7 request-aware draining still must track accepted work.

evidence.quote: During a deployment, draining stops new assignments to A while allowing in-flight work, meaning requests already underway, to finish within a deadline. Shut A down after completion or when that deadline expires.

Stopping new L4 connections does not stop new HTTP requests on existing connections. A drain must also manage those connection lifetimes or stop accepting further requests. L7 request-aware draining must still track already accepted work.
Forced termination at the deadline may interrupt unfinished requests. Their work is not automatically moved to B.

answers.answer: The client sees no response and cannot distinguish a committed purchase with a lost response from an operation that did not complete. Since this purchase committed, a blind retry at B could apply its effect again. Assign one stable idempotency key to the logical purchase and reuse it on every attempt. All backends need a shared durable key-and-result record. In one database transaction reserve the key uniquely, apply the purchase effect, and record its result, committing all or none. A repeat returns the stored result without another purchase effect. Separate checking and writing can race or leave a crash gap. A fresh key fails to identify the same operation; A-only memory cannot reliably protect a retry at B. Bound attempts and delay retries because they consume capacity and can worsen overload; retry policy neither replaces duplicate protection nor guarantees success.

evidence.quote: A backend commits a write, but its response is lost. The client cannot tell whether the write completed. A blind retry on another backend can repeat the effect.
A stable ID for one logical operation, reused on every attempt.

All backends use a shared durable record of the key and result. In one database transaction, reserve the key uniquely, apply the effect and record the result; commit all or none. A repeat returns the recorded result without applying the effect again. Separate check-then-write steps can race or leave a crash gap.
A new key per retry, or a key remembered only in one server's memory, cannot reliably protect retries elsewhere.
Bound retry attempts and delay them: extra requests consume capacity and can deepen overload.
